name: Bro split

card.summary: A weekly routine that trains one muscle group per day; widely used in bodybuilding culture, with no cited research ranking it against other splits.
card.note: Encyclopedic sources cite no comparative research on training splits; the frequency research summarised there concerns muscle groups trained twice weekly versus once.

quick.overview:
The bro split is a way of organising weight training in which each session focuses on one muscle group, for example chest one day, back another, then shoulders, arms and legs. Wikipedia lists it among the common splits alongside full body, upper/lower and push/pull/legs [1].

It is associated with bodybuilding culture and is discussed in lifting forums as a classic arrangement. The wiki found no comparative studies of splits in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: A split divides weekly training volume across muscle groups and days [1]. In a bro split each muscle group is typically trained directly about once per week. Wikipedia's summary of frequency research says two sessions per week produced greater muscle growth than one, while strength gains were not influenced by frequency when total volume was equal [1][2].
quick.risks: No harms specific to the bro split are documented in the sources consulted. General resistance-training cautions, such as overtraining with excessive volume, apply [3].

lead: The bro split is a weekly training split in which each session focuses on a different muscle group, for example chest on one day, back on another, then shoulders, arms and legs. It is the classic bodybuilding arrangement and is used to build muscle size and a more developed, proportioned physique, with each muscle trained hard and then given the rest of the week to recover [1][2].

Wikipedia lists it among the common splits alongside full body, upper/lower and push/pull/legs, and defines a split as how a lifter divides weekly volume across muscle groups and days [1]. The name is slang from lifting communities. Bodybuilding coverage describes growth as depending on training, nutrition and adequate rest, and notes the recovery window after a workout, which is the logic followers give for hitting one body part per day [3].

Research relevant to the bro split concerns training frequency and weekly volume. Wikipedia's summary reports that two sessions per week per muscle group produced greater muscle growth than one, and that with equal volume, frequency did not influence strength gains [1][2]. A 2022 umbrella review of 14 meta-analyses concluded that weekly set volume per muscle group was a key variable for hypertrophy [4].

chain: One muscle group trained with high volume per session
Each group rests for the rest of the week
Muscle grows and physique becomes fuller and more developed
angle.text: Lifters use the bro split to pile focused volume onto one muscle group at a time, with the aim of building bigger, more defined muscles. The look it targets is the classic bodybuilder physique with developed chest, back, shoulders, arms and legs.

infobox: One muscle group (or pair) emphasised per session [1]
About one direct session per muscle group per week

paras: A split is the way a trainee divides weekly volume across muscle groups and days. Wikipedia lists the bro split among common examples, and notes that some programs alternate splits from week to week [1]. In a typical bro split a lifter trains chest on one day, back on another, shoulders and arms on others and legs on another, usually with a rest day or two. Many sessions pair a large muscle with a small one or give each group a full session of several exercises.

Body-part training is tied to bodybuilding, a sport whose competitive federation, the IFBB, was founded in 1946 by Joe and Ben Weider, and whose magazines popularised named training principles in the 1950s and 1960s [3]. The name 'bro split' is community slang rather than a formal term.

Wikipedia's summary of strength-training research reports that more weekly sessions generally yield larger strength gains but that frequency had no influence when total volume was equalised, and that two sessions per week outperformed one for muscle growth, with three versus two unresolved [1][2]. Wikipedia's hypertrophy article states that frequency, intensity and total volume directly affect hypertrophy, with total volume and progressive overload mattering over the long term [5].

A 2022 umbrella review in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living pooled 14 meta-analyses covering 178 primary studies and 4,784 participants. Its authors concluded that around 10 or more weekly sets per muscle group appears beneficial, that eccentric contractions seem important, and that exercise order, time of day and periodisation type did not appear to directly affect muscle gain [4]. How these findings apply to any single split depends on how many weekly sets and sessions a given routine allocates to each muscle.

No harms specific to the bro split are documented. General resistance-training cautions apply: bodybuilding coverage lists overtraining as arising when workload exceeds recovery capacity, often with poor nutrition or too little sleep [3].
No studies found comparing the bro split directly with other splits in the material reviewed. Related research on training frequency and weekly volume is summarised above [1][2][4].

timeline.event: IFBB founded by Joe and Ben Weider; bodybuilding magazines later popularise training principles in the 1950s and 1960s.[3]
